title: Performance gotchas
summary: The handful of things that make Python slow, and the fixes.

steps.title: Pick the right container
body: Python is slower than C# per operation, so **algorithmic** mistakes hurt more. The big ones:
| `x in c` | O(n), scans | O(1), hashed |
clean = [u for u in users if u not in banned]   # fast lookups
`x in list` inside a loop turns O(n) into O(n²). This is the single most common Python slowdown.

steps.prompt: You check 100,000 ids against a list of 50,000 allowed ids with `if i in allowed`. The best fix?
options: Convert `allowed` to a `set` once, before the loop
steps.explain: Sorting does not speed up `in` on a list; it still scans. A set turns each check into a hash lookup.

steps.title: Strings and building results
body: Strings are immutable, so `s += piece` in a loop can copy the growing string every time. Collect pieces and `join` once, which is exactly why C# has `StringBuilder`:
Similarly, prefer built-ins (`sum`, `sorted`, `max`, comprehensions): they run in C inside the interpreter and beat hand-written loops.

steps.prompt: Fast or slow pattern (for large inputs)?

steps.title: Copies, laziness and measuring
body: - Slicing copies: `xs[1:]` in a recursive function copies the list at every level. Pass an index instead.
- Generators avoid building big intermediate lists: `sum(len(l) for l in f)` streams a file.
- `sorted` inside a loop sorts again each time; sort once, outside.
- **Measure, do not guess**: `python -m timeit "..."` or the `timeit` module, and `cProfile` for whole programs.
timeit.timeit("x in s", setup="s = set(range(10000)); x = 9999", number=1000)

code: squares_list = [n * n for n in range(10_000)]
squares_gen = (n * n for n in range(10_000))
steps.explain: The list holds 10,000 references; the generator holds only its paused state, a couple of hundred bytes, whatever the length.
